name: Xorcerer's Stones
description: Misha had been banned from playing chess for good since he was accused of cheating with an engine. Therefore, he retired and decided to become a xorcerer. One day, while taking a walk in a park, Misha came across a rooted tree with nodes numbered from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$. The root of the tree is node $$$1$$$. For each $$$1\le i\le n$$$, node $$$i$$$ contains $$$a_i$$$ stones in it. Misha has recently learned a new spell in his xorcery class and wants to test it out. A spell consists of: Choose some node $$$i$$$ ($$$1 \leq i \leq n$$$). Calculate the bitwise XOR $$$x$$$ of all $$$a_j$$$ such that node $$$j$$$ is in the subtree of $$$i$$$ ($$$i$$$ belongs to its own subtree). Set $$$a_j$$$ equal to $$$x$$$ for all nodes $$$j$$$ in the subtree of $$$i$$$. Misha can perform at most $$$2n$$$ spells and he wants to remove all stones from the tree. More formally, he wants $$$a_i=0$$$ to hold for each $$$1\leq i \leq n$$$. Can you help him perform the spells? A tree with $$$n$$$ nodes is a connected acyclic graph which contains $$$n-1$$$ edges. The subtree of node $$$i$$$ is the set of all nodes $$$j$$$ such that $$$i$$$ lies on the simple path from $$$1$$$ (the root) to $$$j$$$. We consider $$$i$$$ to be contained in its own subtree.
input_specification: The first line contains a single integer $$$n$$$ ($$$2 \leq n \leq 2\cdot 10^5$$$) — the size of the tree The second line contains an array of integers $$$a_1,a_2,\ldots, a_n$$$ ($$$0 \leq a_i \leq 31$$$), describing the number of stones in each node initially. The third line contains an array of integers $$$p_2,p_3,\ldots, p_n$$$ ($$$1 \leq p_i \leq i-1$$$), where $$$p_i$$$ means that there is an edge connecting $$$p_i$$$ and $$$i$$$.
output_specification: If there is not a valid sequence of spells, output $$$-1$$$. Otherwise, output a single integer $$$q$$$ ($$$0 \leq q \leq 2n$$$) in the first line — the number of performed spells. In the second line output a sequence of integers $$$v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_q$$$ ($$$1 \leq v_i \leq n$$$) — the $$$i$$$-th spell will be performed on the subtree of node $$$v_i$$$. Please note that order matters. If multiple solutions exist, output any. You don't have to minimize the number of operations.
approach_summary: Define tree DP state dp[u][state] computing optimal subproblem values for the subtree rooted at u. Aggregate transitions across children in post-order traversal in O(N × S) time.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1779F — Xorcerer's Stones [463. DP on Trees and DAGs]
topic_editorial.summary: Tree Dynamic Programming with post-order traversal.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: A rooted tree has a clean hierarchical structure: removing the root decomposes the tree into independent disjoint subtrees. Therefore, the optimal solution for a subtree rooted at vertex $u$ depends purely on the solutions of its direct children $v \in \text{children}(u)$.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Root Selection & State Definition
Arbitrarily root the tree at node $1$. Define:
- $dp[u][0] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is excluded.
- $dp[u][1] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is included.

### Step 2: Post-Order DFS Traversal
We traverse the tree using depth-first search. A node $u$ computes its answers only after all its children $v \in \text{adj}[u]$ have computed theirs:
$$\text{dfs}(u, \text{parent})$$

### Step 3: Subtree Transition
For each child $v$ of $u$ ($v \ne \text{parent}$):
$$dp[u][0] = \sum_{v} \max(dp[v][0], dp[v][1])$$
$$dp[u][1] = \text{val}[u] + \sum_{v} dp[v][0]$$

### Step 4: Final Answer
At the root:
$$\text{Ans} = \max(dp[1][0], dp[1][1])$$
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Each node and edge in the tree is visited exactly once during the DFS traversal. All transitions at node $u$ run in time proportional to its degree. Summing across all vertices: $\sum \text{deg}(u) = 2(N-1) = \mathcal{O}(N)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Adjacency list storage takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, DP state arrays take $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, and the DFS call stack takes at most $\mathcal{O}(N)$ depth in the worst case.
